title: CSV Transaction Stats
description: Parse → group → aggregate pipeline in TypeScript: `.map` the CSV lines into header-keyed records (collection-transform), then a `for...of` upsert loop that dispatches on a `'DEPOSIT' | 'WITHDRAWAL'` union into a per-company stats class — the loop carries create-if-absent state and mutates an instance, so it is algorithm shape, not a fold.

conversation.intro: The 45-minute 'here's a CSV, aggregate it' interview, in TypeScript. It looks like a parsing problem and is really a data-modeling problem: the interviewer is watching whether you hard-code column indices, whether you coerce the strings, whether your enum dispatch lives in one place — and, in a typed codebase, whether you know which of your guarantees survive to runtime. Each section has what you'd say out loud and why the move matters.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Pin the input format and the output contract before writing a single split.
sections.say:
"So I'm given CSV text — a header row plus data rows — where each row is a transaction with a company, a type that's one of DEPOSIT or WITHDRAWAL, and an amount. I need to roll those up per company into a stats object: total deposited, total withdrawn, transaction count, and net. Output is one line per company, ordered by net descending."

Then the clarifiers, and each one changes the code:
• Can fields contain commas or quotes? If yes, `split(',')` is wrong and I need a real CSV parser (or a quote-aware scanner). For an interview I'd confirm the simple case and say out loud that production would use a library.
• Is the header guaranteed present, and is column ORDER guaranteed? If order can change, I must key off the header names rather than positions.
• Are amounts integers, or dollars-and-cents? Floats push me to integer cents internally.
• What do I do with an unrecognized `type` value — skip it, throw, or bucket it as 'other'?
• Should a company that appears only in withdrawals still show up? (Yes, with deposited 0.)
sections.why: The comma-inside-quotes question is the one that separates candidates. `split(',')` on `Acme, Inc.,DEPOSIT,100` silently produces four wrong cells and every downstream total is garbage with no error. Asking it takes five seconds and tells the interviewer you've parsed real files. The column-order question is what justifies the header-keyed record — if you don't ask it, building the header map looks like over-engineering; if you do ask it, it looks like judgment. And the unknown-type question is what makes the `else throw` in the class defensible rather than arbitrary.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the naive version so the pipeline reads as a choice, not a reflex.
sections.say:
"The naive version is: collect the distinct company names first, then for each company re-scan every row summing deposits and then re-scan again summing withdrawals. That's O(n·k) with three passes and it's genuinely fine for a few thousand rows.

But it re-reads the input once per company, and worse, it spreads the DEPOSIT/WITHDRAWAL knowledge across multiple loops — if a third type shows up later, I have to remember to update every one of them. A single pass that upserts into a per-company accumulator does it in O(n), and it puts the type dispatch in exactly one place. That second reason is the one I actually care about."
sections.why: Most candidates justify the one-pass version purely on complexity. The stronger argument here is maintainability: the enum dispatch is the thing that will change (a TRANSFER type, a FEE type), and centralizing it is a design win independent of n. Leading with that is a senior signal, because the interviewer's follow-up is almost always 'now add a third transaction type' — and you've already explained why your structure absorbs it.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern — header-keyed parse + upsert-into-class
sections.prompt: Three distinct moves: zip against the header, upsert, dispatch.
sections.say:
"There are three separable moves here, and I'll write them as three pieces.

First, the parse. `text.trim().split('\n')` gives lines; destructuring `const [header, ...rows]` peels the header off. `cols = header.split(',')` is my column-name list. Then each data row becomes `Object.fromEntries(cols.map((col, i) => [col, cells[i]]))` — I zip the header names against the cell values so I can write `row.company` instead of `cells[1]`. That's the whole point: if the CSV grows a column or reorders, my code doesn't care.

Second, the grouping. A `Map` keyed by company name, value is a `CompanyStats` instance. The upsert is `if (!map.has(k)) map.set(k, new CompanyStats(k))`, then `map.get(k).apply(...)`. Note this is NOT the `map.get(k) || 0` idiom you'd use for a numeric fold — with an object you must store the instance before mutating it, otherwise you mutate a throwaway.

Third, the dispatch. `apply(type, amount)` branches on the enum: DEPOSIT adds to `deposited`, WITHDRAWAL adds to `withdrawn`, anything else throws. The count increments regardless. `net` is a getter so it's always derived, never a fourth field that can drift out of sync with the other two."
sections.why: The `net` getter is the detail worth volunteering. If `net` were a stored field you'd have to remember to update it in both enum arms, and the moment someone adds a third arm and forgets, your net is silently wrong. Deriving it means it cannot drift — that's the same 'single source of truth' instinct that makes the centralized dispatch worth having. Interviewers reliably notice when a candidate chooses derived-over-stored and can say why.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk enough rows to prove the upsert and the dispatch both fire.
sections.intro: "Let me run this." Three inputs: the full prompt CSV, a single-row degenerate case, and a case where a withdrawal pushes one company below another so the sort actually does work.

examples.input: Full CSV — 5 rows, Acme x3 and Globex x2
examples.note: Acme deposits 1200 and 800 and withdraws 450 across 3 transactions -> net 1550. Globex deposits 900 and withdraws 300 across 2 -> net 600. Sorted by net descending puts Acme first.
examples.trace:
cols = [date, company, type, amount]
row0 Acme/DEPOSIT/1200    -> no Acme yet -> new CompanyStats('Acme')   -> deposited 1200, txns 1
row1 Globex/WITHDRAWAL/300 -> no Globex yet -> new CompanyStats('Globex') -> withdrawn 300, txns 1
row2 Acme/WITHDRAWAL/450   -> Acme exists -> withdrawn 450, txns 2
row3 Globex/DEPOSIT/900    -> Globex exists -> deposited 900, txns 2
row4 Acme/DEPOSIT/800      -> Acme exists -> deposited 2000, txns 3
nets: Acme 2000-450 = 1550, Globex 900-300 = 600
sort desc -> [Acme, Globex] ✓

examples.note: Degenerate case. Proves the upsert creates on first sight and that a company with zero withdrawals still prints `-0` from the constructor default rather than `-undefined`.
examples.trace:
cols = [company, type, amount] (no date column -- the header-keyed parse doesn't care)
row0 Acme/DEPOSIT/500 -> has('Acme') false -> set new CompanyStats('Acme')
  apply('DEPOSIT', 500) -> txns 1, deposited 500, withdrawn stays 0
net = 500 - 0 = 500
sort over 1 entry is a no-op ✓

examples.input: Withdrawal flips the order — Acme +100/-100, Beta +300
examples.note: Acme is seen FIRST but sorts LAST, because its withdrawal cancels its deposit. This is the case that proves we sort on net rather than on insertion order or on deposits alone.
examples.trace:
row0 Acme/DEPOSIT/100    -> new Acme  -> deposited 100, txns 1
row1 Beta/DEPOSIT/300    -> new Beta  -> deposited 300, txns 1
row2 Acme/WITHDRAWAL/100 -> Acme      -> withdrawn 100, txns 2
nets: Acme 100-100 = 0, Beta 300-0 = 300
Map insertion order is [Acme, Beta]; sort by net desc -> [Beta, Acme] ✓

sections.why: The third example is the one to walk out loud, because it's the only one where the sort changes anything — with the first example the Map order and the sorted order coincide, so a bug in the comparator would pass unnoticed. Picking an input where insertion order and output order DISAGREE is a testing instinct worth showing: you deliberately chose data that can distinguish a correct comparator from a missing one.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.say:
"The failure modes I'd call out:
• String amounts. Every CSV cell is a string, so `'1200' + '800'` is `'1200800'`, not 2000 — and it never throws. `Number(row.amount)` at the boundary is load-bearing. I'd also consider guarding `Number.isNaN` for a malformed cell.
• Trailing newline. `'a\nb\n'.split('\n')` gives a final empty string, which parses into a record of `undefined` fields and then quietly creates a company named `undefined`. `text.trim()` before the split kills it.
• Windows line endings. `\r\n` leaves a stray `\r` on the last cell of every row, so `'1200\r'` -> `Number` gives 1200 (it tolerates the whitespace) but a trailing `\r` on a *company* name creates two distinct keys that look identical when printed. Splitting on `/\r?\n/` is the fix.
• The mutate-a-throwaway bug: `const s = map.get(k) || new CompanyStats(k); s.apply(...)` looks equivalent to the upsert but never stores the new instance, so every first transaction per company is silently dropped.
• Unknown type — I throw, which surfaces upstream schema drift immediately. If the requirement is resilience over strictness I'd instead count it into an `other` bucket and log, but silently ignoring it is the one option I'd argue against.
• Duplicate company names differing only in case or whitespace ('Acme' vs 'acme ') split into two buckets. If the data is dirty I'd normalize the key with `.trim().toLowerCase()` while keeping the original for display."
sections.why: The mutate-a-throwaway bug is the one to raise unprompted, because it's the trap specific to accumulating OBJECTS rather than numbers. Everyone has internalized `(map.get(k) || 0) + x` from numeric group-bys, and transplanting that habit to an instance produces code that looks right, runs without error, and is wrong. Naming it shows you know why the object case needs a different idiom instead of pattern-matching on the shape of the previous problem.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: Defend the bound and name what you'd change for a real file.
sections.say:
"Time is O(n + k log k): one pass over n rows with O(1) Map operations and O(c) work per row for the c columns, then a sort over the k distinct companies. Since k <= n and usually k << n, the parse dominates. Space is O(n) for the parsed records plus O(k) for the Map — and honestly the O(n) records array is the part I'd change first at scale.

For a genuinely large file I wouldn't materialize the records at all: stream line by line and fold straight into the Map, which drops peak memory to O(k). The rest of the structure survives that change unmodified, which is a decent sign the decomposition is right.

The transferable shape here is 'flat rows in, keyed aggregates out' — the same skeleton handles orders by customer, log lines by status code, or timesheets by project. What varies is the key function and what the accumulator does per row; the parse-zip-upsert-dispatch spine stays put."
sections.why: Volunteering that the intermediate array is the scaling bottleneck — and that the fix is streaming — answers the follow-up before it's asked, and it's a genuine tradeoff rather than a rehearsed line: materializing is more debuggable and testable, streaming is what you need at a million rows. Noting that the rest of the code survives the change is the real point, because it's evidence that the three moves were separable for a reason.

sections.title: 7. Typing it — what TypeScript actually buys here
sections.prompt: Three modeling decisions, and the one place the type system can't help you.
sections.say:
"Three calls I'd make and defend.

First, the transaction type is a union of string literals — `type TxnType = 'DEPOSIT' | 'WITHDRAWAL'` — not an `enum`. Both check callers just as tightly, but a union is erased completely while an `enum` generates a real runtime object. In a codebase that's already shipping JSON strings over the wire, the union is also the thing that matches the data: I'm comparing against the literal `'DEPOSIT'` either way, so introducing an enum member that merely wraps that string adds a translation layer for nothing.

Second, `CsvRow.amount` is typed `string`, not `number`. That's deliberate and it's the honest model — a CSV cell IS text. Typing it `number` would be a lie the compiler happily believes, and then `Number()` looks redundant right up until the totals come out concatenated.

Third — and this is the one I'd make sure to say out loud — the types do not validate the file. `Object.fromEntries(...) as CsvRow` is a cast, and a cast is an assertion, not a check: I'm telling the compiler to believe a shape it has no way to verify. So the union constrains my code and the guard constrains the data. `function isTxnType(v: string): v is TxnType` does both jobs at once — it's a real runtime comparison, and the `v is TxnType` return type narrows the value for everything downstream."
sections.why: The compile-time versus runtime boundary is the thing interviewers are actually probing when they hand a typed candidate untrusted input, and it's where confident TypeScript users most often slip: the cast reads like a guarantee, so the guard gets skipped, and the failure is silent because the erased union can't object. Naming the cast as an assertion rather than a check — and then showing the type guard as the piece that bridges back — demonstrates you know exactly how much of your safety survives `tsc`. The enum-versus-union argument is the secondary signal: preferring the zero-emit option, and being able to say why, reads as someone who has thought about what their types compile to rather than just satisfying the checker.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the parse-group-aggregate pipeline on real CSV text. The state panel shows the parsed `cols`, the header-keyed `rows`, and the `byCompany` Map as each transaction is applied. Watch which rows CREATE a stats instance versus mutate an existing one, and watch `net` recompute as withdrawals land.

reference.approach: Header-keyed parse → Map upsert → union-typed dispatch into a stats class
notes: TypeScript types are ERASED before the code runs — they cost nothing at runtime and change no behavior. Everything below is still the same JavaScript algorithm.
`type TxnType = 'DEPOSIT' | 'WITHDRAWAL'` is a union of string literals. Prefer it to `enum`: it checks callers just as tightly but emits no runtime code, whereas an `enum` generates a real object.

Because types are erased, the union does NOT validate the CSV. `isTxnType` — a type guard, signalled by the `value is TxnType` return type — is what actually checks the untrusted text, and it also narrows the type for the compiler.
`as CsvRow` is an unchecked cast: it changes what the compiler believes, not what exists. That's the precise reason the runtime guard is still required after it.

Objects need a real upsert: `if (!map.has(k)) map.set(k, new X(k))` then mutate. The numeric `map.get(k) || 0` habit fails here — `map.get(k) || new X(k)` mutates an instance that was never stored, silently dropping every company's first transaction.

`Number(row.amount)` is still load-bearing: `CsvRow.amount` is typed `string` because CSV cells ARE strings, so TypeScript would reject `+= row.amount` at compile time — but nothing coerces it for you at runtime.
`net` is a getter, not a stored field — derived values can't drift out of sync when a new enum arm forgets to update them.

questions.q: Why is the upsert written as `if (!byCompany.has(k)) byCompany.set(k, new CompanyStats(k))` rather than the shorter `const s = byCompany.get(k) || new CompanyStats(k)`?
options: `Map.get` throws on a missing key, so it must be guarded by `has` before any read
The `||` form builds an instance that is never stored in the Map, so every company's first transaction is applied to a throwaway object and lost
`Map.set` refuses to overwrite an existing key, so `has` must be checked to avoid a silent no-op
Class instances are always falsy until their constructor returns, which makes `||` pick the wrong branch
questions.explain: With numbers, `map.get(k) || 0` works because you write the result back with `set`. With an object you mutate in place — so if the new instance was never stored, the mutation lands on an orphan and the Map still has no entry for that company.

questions.q: `CsvRow.amount` is typed `string`, and the code still calls `Number(row.amount)`. Why is the conversion required even though the field is typed?
options: It isn't required — TypeScript coerces a `string` field to `number` automatically when it is used in arithmetic
Types are erased before the code runs, so nothing converts the value at runtime; the annotation only stops you writing `+= row.amount` in the editor
`Number()` is required because `Map` keys must be primitives and the amount is part of the composite key
The cast to `CsvRow` re-tags the field as `number`, so `Number()` merely documents a conversion that already happened
questions.explain: TypeScript's job ends at compile time. The annotation catches the mistake in your editor — `this.deposited += row.amount` is a type error — but at runtime the value is still the string '1200', and `'0' + '1200'` is `'01200'`. The compiler tells you to convert; it never converts for you.

questions.q: Records are built with `Object.fromEntries(cols.map((col, i) => [col, cells[i]]))` instead of reading `cells[1]`, `cells[2]` directly. What does that buy?
options: It removes the need to call `Number()` on the amount, because `fromEntries` infers cell types
It is measurably faster than index access because `fromEntries` builds a hash table in one pass
It guarantees the row has exactly as many cells as the header has columns, throwing otherwise
The aggregation reads columns by NAME, so the CSV can add a column or reorder them without breaking any downstream code
questions.explain: Hard-coded indices couple every downstream line to the exact column layout. Keying off the header row means only the header parse knows about positions.

questions.q: `net` is written as a getter (`get net() { return this.deposited - this.withdrawn; }`) rather than a field updated inside `apply`. Why prefer the getter?
options: Getters are evaluated once at construction, so the value is cached and cheaper to read repeatedly
A stored `net` would have to be updated in every enum arm, so a newly added transaction type that forgets to touch it leaves `net` silently wrong; a derived value cannot drift
Fields assigned in a constructor are not enumerable, so a stored `net` would be invisible to the final `.map`
Only getters can be used inside a `sort` comparator, since comparators receive frozen copies of their operands
questions.explain: Deriving `net` from the two totals makes it impossible for it to disagree with them. A stored copy is a second source of truth that every future code path has to remember to maintain.

questions.q: The code calls `text.trim()` before `split('\n')`. What does that prevent?
options: A leading byte-order mark that would otherwise corrupt the first column name
Amounts with surrounding spaces being rejected by `Number`, which does not tolerate whitespace
A trailing newline producing one extra empty line, which parses into a record of undefined fields and creates a bogus company keyed `undefined`
The header row being included in the data rows, since `split` keeps the separator on the first element
questions.explain:
`'a
b
'.split('
')` yields `['a','b','']`. That empty final line becomes a record whose every field is `undefined`, and the upsert then happily creates a company named `undefined`.

questions.q: `apply` takes `type: TxnType`, a union of the only two legal strings. Why does the code STILL call `isTxnType(row.type)` before passing it?
options: Because a union type only constrains variables, not function parameters, so `apply` would accept any string regardless
Because `isTxnType` also converts the string to the union's underlying numeric representation
Because the union is erased at runtime, so it constrains code the compiler can see — not a CSV file; the guard is the only thing that actually rejects a bad value
Because TypeScript requires an explicit guard before any value may be passed to a parameter with a union type
questions.explain: The compiler can police your own call sites, but the CSV arrives at runtime, long after every type has been deleted. `Object.fromEntries(...) as CsvRow` asserts a shape without verifying it, so `row.type` could be any string at all. The `value is TxnType` guard does two jobs: it performs the real runtime check, and it narrows the type so the compiler accepts the call afterwards.

L3.prompt: In TypeScript: parse a CSV of transactions (`date,company,type,amount` where type is DEPOSIT or WITHDRAWAL), roll them up per company into a stats class tracking deposited, withdrawn and transaction count, and print one line per company ordered by net descending. Model the transaction type as a string-literal union and validate it at the parse boundary.
L3.expectedOutput:
Acme: +2000 / -450 (3 txns) net 1550
Globex: +900 / -300 (2 txns) net 600
hints: Model the type as `type TxnType = 'DEPOSIT' | 'WITHDRAWAL'` rather than an `enum` — same checking, no runtime output.
Peel the header with `const [header, ...rows] = text.trim().split('\n')`, zip each row against `header.split(',')`, and `as CsvRow` the result.
Types are erased at runtime, so validate the untrusted string with a type guard: `function isTxnType(v: string): v is TxnType`.
Upsert the class instance: `if (!map.has(k)) map.set(k, new CompanyStats(k))`, then `map.get(k)!.apply(...)` — mutate the STORED instance.
